Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{2y}{x}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above.
source_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{2y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}{8y}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the below-left quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(0,-1),$ as shown above.
source_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}{8y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+16(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{16({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t\,{|}_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-8(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\pi ) \\  & =-8(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{3x}{y}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-left quarter of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0),$ as shown above.
source_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{3x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }3\operatorname{cot}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-9[\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-9(0-1) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}}{8x}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the lower half of the circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above.
source_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}}{8x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{3}}{8(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{64\operatorname{sin}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{32\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }2\operatorname{tan}⁡t\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =-8[\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ] \\  & =-8(1-(-1)) \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$
